What Thought Leadership Actually Is

Guidelowob research

By lowob · 27 August 2026 · Updated 16 November 2026 · 7-minute read · Growth

Thought leadership is a defensible position, supported by evidence the audience could not assemble, with a consequence for the reader, sustained over time. Buyers say it matters: in the 2026 Edelman-LinkedIn study, 73% of B2B decision makers said useful data or evidence is what makes thought leadership worth sharing, and 59% of final decision makers said poor or absent thought leadership had led to a vendor being dropped. Most of what carries the name is agreeable content measured by impressions. The real thing comes from a founder's or senior operator's actual thinking, on a cadence they can sustain.

Thought leadership is content published to establish a person or a company as an authority: someone whose view of a market is worth seeking out, quoting and acting on. The term has been used so loosely that it now mostly describes LinkedIn posts. The original idea is worth recovering, because the real thing is one of the few marketing assets that compounds.

What it requires

ElementWhat it meansExample of the difference
A positionA specific, defensible claim, not a subjectTopic: "distribution for restricted categories". Position: "the channels the platforms leave to restricted categories are cheaper because the platforms restrict them."
EvidenceObservation, data, experience or examples the audience could not assemble themselvesA position without evidence is an opinion, and the internet has enough
ConsequenceSomething the reader should do differentlyAuthority is earned by being useful, not by being interesting
ConsistencyA body of work returning to the same territory, developing it, being proved right or adjusting when wrongOne good piece is an article; a sustained argument is authority

What buyers say they value

The most useful evidence on this comes from the annual B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report by Edelman and LinkedIn. Both organisations sell services that benefit from more thought leadership spending, so read the figures as buyer opinion gathered by interested parties. The samples are large and the direction has been consistent across editions.

The 2026 edition, published in November 2026, surveyed more than 1,100 business executives in seven countries:

Finding (2026 edition)Share
Used AI to summarise thought leadership during vendor evaluation84%
Said thought leadership helped assess whether a vendor understood their needs76%
Named useful data, research or evidence as what makes it worth sharing73%
Final decision makers who said poor or absent thought leadership led to a vendor being removed59%
Said the strongest trust driver is showing clear understanding of their challenges56%
Said the strongest trust driver is the strength of the product or service14%

The 2025 edition, which surveyed nearly 2,000 professionals including "hidden" buyers outside the formal decision group, found 86% favoured perspectives that challenge their assumptions, and 91% of hidden buyers wanted insights that reveal unseen risks or opportunities. It also found 79% were more likely to champion a vendor in a formal evaluation if it consistently published quality thought leadership.

Three of the four requirements above show up directly in what buyers report: evidence (73%), consequence (understanding their challenges and revealing risks), and position (challenging assumptions). The fourth, consistency, is what "consistently publishes" measures.

Real thought leadership ends with a claim the reader could disagree with. The imitation ends with "the future is exciting and organisations must adapt."

Why most attempts fail

They start from the desire to be seen as a leader rather than from a view. They pick topics that are safe, which means topics where the author agrees with everyone. They avoid specifics for fear of being wrong. They are written by a marketing team imitating an executive who has not supplied any thinking. And they measure themselves by impressions, which rewards being agreeable and punishes being right.

The tell is the ending. Real thought leadership ends with a claim the reader could disagree with.

AI has raised the stakes in two directions. Drafting is now cheap, so agreeable content is abundant; our piece Judgment is the moat covers what that does to differentiation. And the reader is often a model: when 84% of decision makers summarise thought leadership with AI, a piece with no specific claim summarises to nothing. A position with evidence survives compression. A tone does not.

How it differs from content marketing

Content marketing answers questions the audience already has, so that they find the company when searching. Thought leadership raises questions the audience had not thought to ask, so that they seek the company out.

Content marketingThought leadership
Starts fromA question buyers already search forA belief the market currently gets wrong
Asset typeSearch and citation assetReputation asset
Who must supply itAnyone with subject knowledgeSomeone with a view and evidence for it
Success looks likeFound, cited, used at the right buying stageSought out, quoted, argued with
Typical volumeMany piecesFew pieces, sustained

Both are valuable. Most companies need more of the first than they think and less of the second than they produce. Our piece on content with a job covers the first; thought leadership that sales can use covers how to put the second into deals.

How to produce it without a full-time writer

The thinking has to come from a person who has it, usually a founder or a senior operator. That person's time is scarce. The system that works:

  1. A recurring interview. Forty-five minutes, on one question, conducted by someone who challenges abstractions and asks for examples.
  2. A transcript. The raw material, kept.
  3. A short editorial process. AI-assisted extraction and structure, producing a flagship piece and a small set of adaptations, with the founder approving anything in their voice.
  4. A ledger of positions. A record of what the company has argued, so each piece builds on the last rather than starting over.

That system produces a piece every two to four weeks with about two hours of the founder's time. It does not produce daily posts, and it should not try to. Our piece on the founder interview content engine sets out the workflow, and from founder-led to team-led marketing covers what happens when the founder can no longer be the only source.

The test

Before publishing, ask three questions. Could a competent competitor have written this from public information? What would a smart person in the audience disagree with? What should the reader do on Monday? If the answers are yes, nothing and nothing, it is content. It may still be worth publishing. It is not thought leadership.

lowob takeaways

  • Write a position, not a topic. A claim someone could dispute, with evidence they could not assemble.
  • Lead with evidence. It is what buyers say makes thought leadership worth sharing.
  • Write for the summary. If a model compresses your piece, the claim should survive.
  • Sustain it. A cadence the founder can keep beats a burst of volume.

Common questions

What is thought leadership?

Content that establishes a person or company as an authority whose view is worth seeking out and acting on. It needs a defensible position, evidence the audience could not assemble, a consequence for the reader, and consistency over time.

What is the difference between thought leadership and content marketing?

Content marketing answers questions the audience already has, so they find you in search. Thought leadership raises questions they had not thought to ask, so they seek you out.

Does B2B thought leadership influence buying decisions?

Buyers say so. In the 2026 Edelman-LinkedIn study, 76% said it helped them judge whether a vendor understood their needs, and 59% of final decision makers said weak or absent thought leadership had led to a vendor being dropped.

How can a founder produce thought leadership without a full-time writer?

Hold a recurring 45-minute interview on one question, transcribe it, and run a short AI-assisted editorial process with the founder approving anything in their voice. That yields a piece every two to four weeks.
